title: Cristaux (1970). Gribouillis et calculs divers : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page sits in a run of numerical scratch work (pp. 57–59) in the 'Cristaux' folder. Its context is probably slopes of F-crystals, Dieudonné modules and Barsotti–Tate groups, around the time of Grothendieck's 1970 letter to Barsotti and his Montréal lectures. That context is inferred from the folder, not from the page.

The page has three fraction checks and one figure.

Fraction checks:
- 4/5 < 13/15 (0.800 < 0.867).
- 12/14 = 6/7.
- 14/16 = 7/8 <, completed on p. 59 as 13/15 < 7/8.

Figure: axes on squared paper, with one unit about 62 px both ways.
- **Upper line:** runs from the origin to about (16,14). Its slope is 14/16 = 7/8.
- **Lower line:** starts at (1,0) on the horizontal axis, after a short horizontal segment from the origin, and ends about one unit lower, near (16,13). Its slope is 13/15.
- **Dotted lattice points:** they lie between or along the lines at roughly (2,1), (3,2), (4,3), (5,4), (6,5), (7,6), (8,7), then (9,7), (10,8). This is a staircase of unit diagonal steps with an occasional horizontal step, i.e. a lattice path approximating a line of slope near 7/8.
- **Faint lines:** there are also faint auxiliary lines, e.g. from the origin to (2,1).

Interpretation: Grothendieck is comparing a line of slope 7/8 with a line of slope 13/15 that is shifted by one unit (a segment of slope 0, then slope 13/15). He then checks which lattice points (x,y) lie above or below each line by comparing y/x, or y/(x−1), with the slope. Examples are 4/5 against 13/15 here, and 3/4 > 11/15 and 2/3 < 11/16 on p. 59.

Page 57 does the same for denominator 17: values n/17 for n = 1..16, with integer parts ν = 1, 2, 3, and many comparisons of simple fractions with fractions of denominator 17, 23 or 24. This pattern fits two possible purposes:
- computing the best lattice approximation (Christoffel / Sturmian path) to a line of rational slope;
- comparing candidate Newton polygons (polygons with rational slopes and integral break points) with each other, or with Hodge-type integral polygons.

Either would serve to understand the partial order on Newton polygons of F-crystals, e.g. specialization, or which polygons lie between two given ones. The page itself contains no statement, only checks on examples.
errors: No arithmetic errors: 4/5 < 13/15, 12/14 = 6/7, 14/16 = 7/8 and (next page) 13/15 < 7/8 are all correct.
The purpose of the figure cannot be determined with certainty; any link to Newton/Hodge polygons is inferred from the folder context, not stated on the page.

ideas.what: Comparing the polygon through (0,0)–(16,14) (slope 7/8) with a polygon going (0,0)–(1,0) then slope 13/15, and locating lattice points relative to these lines by comparing fractions.
ideas.modern_name: Newton polygons / partial order on Newton polygons (slopes of F-crystals); lattice-point position relative to a line
ideas.usually_credited_to: Dieudonné–Manin (slope classification, 1955/1963); Grothendieck (specialization of Newton polygons, 1970); Katz (1979); Oort (converse, 2000s)
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck, 'Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné' (Montréal 1970, publ. 1974) and letter to Barsotti (1970) discuss Newton polygons and their specialization; this specific numerical example is not published.

ideas.what: Staircase of lattice points approximating a line of slope ~7/8, built from unit diagonal steps with occasional horizontal steps.
ideas.modern_name: Christoffel word / Sturmian lattice path; integral approximation of a rational-slope line (cf. minimal/isoclinic Dieudonné modules of slope m/n)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Christoffel (1875); Manin (1963) for isoclinic Dieudonné modules; Oort (minimal p-divisible groups, 2005)

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only elementary fraction comparisons and a hand-drawn comparison of two nearly parallel rational-slope lines with lattice points. It is consistent with routine example-checking about Newton polygons in the crystals context, with no new statement or construction.
